newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW - Holderbank sees EMU lid on construction.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Holderbank sees EMU lid on construction.

text.p: Cement firm Holderbank sees no major upturn in western Europe's stagnant construction sector as long as public spending is capped by fiscal preparations for the European single currency and major infrastructure projects remain in government hands.

But Thomas Schmidheiny, chairman and chief executive of the world's biggest cement maker, said western Europe would remain a profitable cash-generator for the group under recent plans to trim capacity and streamline its European organisation.

The company, whose full name is Holderbank Financiere Glarus AG, is well-established in the strong U.S. market, Canada and fast-growing Latin America while building a presence in booming southeast Asia and China.
It is also active in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Morocco and Lebanon.
"We don't see a turnaround in (western) Europe as a whole," Schmidheiny told Reuters in a recent interview.
"I am pessimistic in the sense that there will be a stagnation or slight reduction of sales in France and probably Benelux and what have you," he said.
"But on the other hand, I am not pessimistic about our business, about having a strong cash generation and bottom line in Europe."

"But we have to adapt the production and distribution facilities. Our information technology, the number of headquarters of different businesses will be concentrated. All these are the types of measures which we have to go through now," he said.

Holderbank surprised investors and analysts last month by announcing a one-time charge of 607 million Swiss francs on its 1996 accounts, for reorganising in western Europe, slashing net profit after minorities from 493 million Swiss francs to 43 million. In 1995 Holderbank made 450 million Swiss francs net after minorities.
Schmidheiny said only about 10 to 15 percent of the charge would be cash with the rest going for chopping the book value of some assets.

Apart from closing a cement plant in Switzerland for 161 million, Holderbank has not detailed its plans except to say they will take about two years and reduce annual fixed costs by 50 million Swiss francs.
"It will certainly be a whole set of smaller projects, such as integrating activities," Schmidheiny told Reuters.
"Bigger projects we simply cannot talk about because this is a sensitive political and social issue, which we respect."

"So you will see a series of measures taken over the next two years which will lead to more efficient structures, maybe partial closedowns at certain plants if certain products can be more efficiently produced in another plant," he said.
Schmidheiny made clear that Holderbank sees demand for cement, concrete and aggregates as flat in the medium to long term in western Europe.

European Union plans for a single currency from 1999 were a major factor dampening construction as governments chop spending in order to meet deficit limits for joining and remaining in the new currency.
Schmidheiny said another factor was a European tendency to keep major infrasture projects in state hands.

"Infrastructure such as airports, railroads and roads can be given to the private sector to develop. The funds are there, liquidity is very high in the market, interest rates are low and they would be very attractive deals," he said.
"Unfortunately, the vision in Europe that government is the sole provider of infrastructure has to change. And we don't see really that this view is changing."
While demand stagnates in western Europe, good growth is coming from central and eastern European business.
"In the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary we have had a very good start to this year. We are even surprised at the strong markets in this area," Schmidheiny said.
